summary: Specifies an RTP payload format for generic forward error correction of media data, based on XOR parity. It supports different protection lengths, levels and group sizes to suit various media and networks. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5109 defines extra RTP packets that can help a receiver reconstruct lost media. The sender chooses which packets and how much of each packet to protect, so important data can receive stronger protection.

questions: how does xor parity fec work
how does uneven level protection work
subtitle: Adds XOR-based repair data to RTP media packets without changing the original media packets.

tldr.problem: Real-time media usually cannot wait for lost packets to be retransmitted, so a receiver needs repair information sent in advance.
tldr.mechanism: The sender combines selected media packets with XOR and sends FEC packets that identify the protected sequence numbers, lengths and protection levels.
tldr.outcome: The format obsoletes RFC 2733 and RFC 3009 but is not backward compatible with their FEC formats. Receivers that do not support FEC can ignore the additional packets.

today: RFC 5109 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2007. It obsoletes RFC 2733 and RFC 3009; the unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why Real-Time Media Uses FEC
sections.content:
Real-time audio and video often cannot wait for retransmission when a packet is lost. Forward Error Correction (FEC) sends redundant information with the media so a receiver can recover missing data without requesting another copy.

This format uses XOR parity and extends the formats in RFC 2733 and RFC 3009 with protection for different portions of packets. It also corrects their inconsistent use of RTP header fields. The original media packets remain unchanged, so a receiver without FEC support can ignore the additional protection data.
sections.plainLanguage: When media must arrive promptly, asking the sender to retransmit a lost packet may take too long. FEC sends extra information that can help the receiver rebuild missing data locally.

sections.title: XOR Parity and Uneven Protection
sections.content:
The sender combines packet data with the exclusive-or (XOR) operation. If two packets are a and b, a parity packet containing f(a,b) can recover either one when the other packet is available. More parity uses more bandwidth but can protect against more loss.

Uneven Level Protection (ULP) divides each packet into sections, called levels, and protects each section separately. Lower levels can use smaller groups and stronger protection. A single FEC packet can include several levels, and the sender can change each level's protection length during a session.
sections.plainLanguage: XOR lets a receiver combine a parity packet with the media packets it still has to recover missing data. ULP can protect the beginning of a packet more strongly than later parts.

sections.title: Media Packets and FEC Packet Fields
sections.content:
FEC does not alter the format of media packets. An FEC packet contains an RTP header, a 10-octet FEC header, then one or more level headers and parity payloads. Its header records recovery information for RTP fields, a sequence-number base, timestamp recovery, length recovery and whether it uses a short or long mask.

Each level header contains a 16-bit protection length and a mask. A set mask bit identifies a protected media sequence number relative to the sequence-number base. The mask covers 16 packets in its short form or 48 packets in its long form. Level headers are 4 or 8 octets, depending on the mask.
sections.plainLanguage: The FEC packet states which media sequence numbers it covers and how many bytes it protects at each level. The receiver uses those fields to decide which data can be combined.

sections.title: Building Parity and Recovering Packets
sections.content:
The sender applies XOR to selected RTP header bits and packet data. If protected packets have different lengths, shorter data is padded with zero octets before the operation. Each protection level carries only its chosen number of bytes, beginning after the RTP header information represented in the FEC header.

Recovery first determines which available media and FEC packets can reconstruct a lost packet. The receiver then XORs their protected data, restores the RTP header and combines the recovered levels. Depending on which levels can be recovered, the result may contain the whole packet or only part of it.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender builds parity from the selected packet data. To recover a loss, the receiver combines that parity with available packets and rebuilds the missing header and payload portions.

sections.title: Sending FEC and Negotiating It
sections.content:
FEC can travel as a separate RTP stream or as redundant coding alongside media using the redundant-payload format. The sender signals which transport it uses, for example through SDP, and uses a dynamic RTP payload type for FEC.

For a separate stream, the FEC RTP header uses the protected stream's SSRC and its own consecutive sequence numbers. For redundant encoding, the FEC protects the primary media codec. The specification registers audio, video, text and application ULPFEC media subtypes. In offer/answer negotiation, an answerer can reject FEC while accepting the media.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender can put FEC in a separate RTP stream or include it as redundant coding with media. The peers signal the choice, while the media packet format itself stays unchanged.

sections.title: Security and Congestion
sections.content:
FEC may be applied before or after encryption. When encryption is used, applications SHOULD encrypt both media and FEC streams, and separate streams MUST use different keys. The RFC warns that altered FEC fields can produce incorrect recovery and recommends checks before and after reconstruction.

Sending more FEC as packet loss rises can worsen congestion. Implementations MUST NOT substantially increase total media-plus-FEC bandwidth as losses increase. The RFC also requires attention to congestion behavior and fairness with TCP traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: FEC data needs protection because changing it can make a receiver reconstruct incorrect media. Adding more repair traffic during congestion can make the congestion worse.
